items.title: These five divisions define how far we can go in space
items.summary: In this Universe, just because you can see it doesn’t mean you can reach it. Conversely, just because you can’t see it today doesn’t necessarily mean that its light won’t arrive tomorrow. Because the fabric of the Universe itself is expanding, and because the maximum speed at which any signal — whether massive or massless — can travel through that fabric of space is finite, there are both: places that we can currently see that we could never reach or communicate with, and places that we cannot currently observe today, but whose light is on the way and will someday reach us in the future. Today, there’s a well-understood limit for how far we can observe in any direction in space: 46.1 billion light-years. That limit is the size of the presently observable Universe, and it’s set by the combination of the initial expansion rate at the start of the hot Big Bang, the matter-and-energy contents of the Universe, the amount of time that’s elapsed since the hot Big Bang occurred, and the value of the maximum signal speed through space: the speed of light. Inside of the presently observable Universe is a smaller region that, if we sent a signal or a spacecraft today, could someday reach objects within that volume: the reachability or communicability limit. Outside of the presently observable Universe is a larger region whose light will someday arrive at our eyes: the future visibility limit. And beyond that limit lies the unobservable Universe, whose true extent is unknown. Here’s what defines those four key regions, and what might change our current ways of thinking. This illustration shows galaxies receding mutually away from one another within the expanding Universe: a consequence of both the Big Bang and the late-time onset of dark energy. Although the expansion has been occurring continuously ever since the Big Bang, the fact that we see the expansion ongoing today doesn’t necessarily mean we can extrapolate everything back to a singular point in space and time in our Universe’s past. Credit : Mark Garlick/Science Photo Library There are several keys to understanding how far we can reach and how far we can see at any point in the history of the Universe, but they all require us to begin with two key concepts: the idea of the expanding Universe and the framework of the hot Big Bang. When most of us think of expansion, we think about something stretching and becoming thinner: like the skin of a balloon that’s being blown up. The Universe isn’t actually like that, however. As space itself expands, nothing about it thins or changes; there’s simply more of it than there was at the beginning. The matter and energy that’s within it can become less dense — keeping the number of particles the same while increasing the volume — but the space itself is no different after expanding than before. What can change, however, is the rate of expansion itself. The rate of expansion is related to the (square root of the) total energy density of space at any given moment. As the Universe expands, the component of energy inherent to space itself (dark energy) remains constant and doesn’t dilute, but the portions that are made of matter and radiation do dilute, getting less dense. As a result, the expansion rate drops as the energy density drops, causing the Universe to expand more and more slowly as time goes on. How matter (top), radiation (middle), and dark energy/inflationary energy (bottom) all evolve with time in an expanding Universe. As the Universe expands, the matter density dilutes, but the radiation also becomes cooler as its wavelengths get stretched to longer, less energetic states. Dark energy’s (or inflationary energy’s) density, on the other hand, will truly remain constant if it behaves as is currently thought: as a form of energy intrinsic to space itself. These three components, together, dictate how the Universe expands at all times from the Big Bang until the present day and beyond. Credit : E. Siegel/Beyond The Galaxy The Big Bang, meanwhile, is normally visualized incorrectly : as a singularity, or the birth of time and space, where all of the matter and energy in the Universe was compressed into a single point. That’s not necessarily true and hasn’t been thought to be the case for over 45 years: since cosmic inflation was first proposed. We now recognize that the Big Bang represents the hot, dense, early state associated with our Universe as-we-know-it in its infancy, but that state was preceded and set up by an earlier state: cosmic inflation , where there was no matter or radiation in the Universe, but only an enormous amount of that relentless energy inherent to space itself. In the aftermath of inflation, the hot Big Bang commenced. The Universe began expanding extremely rapidly, as the density during those early moments was tremendous. As it expanded, however: the density dropped, the kinetic energy of each matter particle and the energy of each radiation particle decreased, causing the Universe to expand more and more slowly as time went on. Eventually, the energy density in the form of radiation drops below the total energy density in the form of matter: a transition that occurs a few thousand years after the Big Bang. Neutral atoms form, gravitation leads to black holes, stars, galaxies, and a cosmic web, and eventually, the matter density drops so low that the energy inherent to space itself — today’s dark energy — becomes the dominant form of energy that determines the expansion of the Universe, a transition which occurred about 6 billion years ago. The relative importance of different energy components in the Universe at various times in the past. Dark matter has been largely important for extremely long cosmic times, and we can see its signatures in even the Universe’s earliest signals. Meanwhile, radiation was dominant for the first ~10,000 years of the Universe after the Big Bang. Note that in the future, when dark energy reaches a number near 100%, the energy density of the Universe (and, therefore, the expansion rate) will remain constant arbitrarily far ahead in time. Credit: E. Siegel Throughout all this time, the amount of Universe that an observer can potentially see has been increasing. We can imagine that, at the onset of the hot Big Bang, from every point in the Universe an enormous amount of omnidirectional radiation emerged. At any other point, you’ll see that initially-emitted light arriving from a spherical surface surrounding you based on the speed of light, the expansion of the Universe, and the amount of time that’s elapsed since the hot Big Bang first occurred. Back when a total time of: 1 picosecond had elapsed, that sphere was about the size of the Earth-Sun distance, 1 millisecond had elapsed, that sphere was about the size of one light-year, 1 second had elapsed, that sphere was about the size of a massive globular cluster, around 20-40 light-years in radius, 1 year had elapsed, the Universe was just a little bit smaller than the radius of the Milky Way, 10,000 years had elapsed, the now matter-dominated Universe was about 10 million light-years in radius, 13.8 billion years had elapsed, bringing us up to our dark energy-dominated present, the Universe is 46.1 billion light-years in radius. It is precisely this line of thinking that leads us to draw conclusions about the size of the observable Universe at any moment in cosmic history: the amount of distance that light generated at the start of the hot Big Bang could have traveled from that event and still reach us. The scale of the Universe (y-axis) versus the age of the Universe (x-axis) on logarithmic scales. Some size and time milestones are marked, as appropriate. Everything contained within the entire observable Universe was once contained in a very small volume, as shown by the size scale on the y-axis. Credit: E. Siegel Howev

items.title: The world hasn’t become less smelly — we’ve just lost our nasal knowledge
items.summary: Air, land, and sea. Our world is characterized by a proliferating variety of uncertain scents. Yet our noses are ill-equipped to discern between them. Pollution, pandemics, and poverty have conspired to reduce our sensitivity. Some gases, such as the rotten-egg stink of hydrogen sulfide emitted by industries and waste sites, induce a selective loss of smell. These substances are most dangerous when they are least odorous. When we try to use our noses, the result can be confusion. Supermarkets across the globe have begun to remove “best before” dates from products such as milk and yogurt in an attempt to avoid food waste. They have encouraged consumers to deploy the sniff test to distinguish the sweet, mild, scent of fresh milk from a sour spoiled odor. Sniffing was one of the main ways in which premodern people could discern the freshness of food; but thanks to the arrival of cellophane packaging and refrigeration, we have allowed our nasal knowledge to deteriorate. Many consumers still confuse the “best before” date, a measure of quality, with the “use by” date, a measure of safety, and end up endangering themselves by relying on the nose too much or wasting food by relying on it too little. When it comes to the olfactory — the scientific term for all things smell-related — we are living in a land of confusion. One reason that we seldom rely on our sense of smell is that we value it so little. In response to a 2011 worldwide survey of 7,000 16- to 30-year-olds, over half said they would give up their sense of smell before handing over their technology. Ten years later, a survey of 407 college students and adults in the U.S. found that one-quarter of the college student respondents said that they would give up their sense of smell in order to keep their phone, and nearly half of all women would give up their sense of smell to keep their hair. We also generally believe that humans are poor smellers. There are expert sniffers among the human population who describe the odors of wines, coffees, and perfumes. But we do not teach our children how to use their noses. Schools are places in which odors are feared as signs of hygiene poverty, where children learn that cleanliness is a civic duty, and where the young come to understand that those who smell different should be excluded. As the world of smells expands and shape-shifts, we have become trapped in a vicious cycle in which olfactory illiteracy and a disinclination to deploy our noses mutually reinforce each other. Yet there is hope. The last few years have seen a renewed interest in all things olfactory. The recent, anosmia-inducing COVID-19 pandemic and the rise of digital worlds that lack scent have made people aware of what it means to lose our sense of smell. Social media is alive with communities sharing their favorite fragrances. Museums and attractions are embracing scent as they attempt to engage audiences through all of their senses. But the popular discussion of smell’s past is dominated by a narrative of decline and disappearance. Books on the science of smell have multiplied. But many of these contain statements that would make historians blush. One claims that “the stench of cities decreased in the nineteenth century.” The question of which cities and whose assessment of stench aside, this somewhat underestimates the impact of the flushing toilet, industrial expansion, and the massive growth of horse-bound transportation. We are often told that the modern world is one that has devalued the sense of smell whilst deodorizing the world around us. I want to offer a different story. The past and the present are both rich in smells. In fact, over the course of the last few centuries, our world has been odorized in new and ever more opaque ways. We have not forgotten the sense of smell and the world has not necessarily become less odorous, but it has become less easily navigable by nose. Understanding the smells of the past can help us escape our present disorientation and equip our noses for the planet’s challenging future. In the spring of 2022, I set out to discover what people in Britain thought of the smells around them and which scents from their lives they wanted to preserve for the future. Since the 1930s, Mass Observation has been dedicated to tracing the everyday experiences and attitudes of the British public, but they had never asked the public about smell. We challenged their participants, who had signed up to respond to the archive’s quarterly “directives,” to perform three tasks: to talk about the smell of a significant object in their home, to record a smell diary of an ordinary day, and to reflect on the smells that had meant something to them over the course of their lives. Many of the respondents struggled to describe an odorous object in their homes. People were puzzled by the smell diary, though certain patterns did emerge: the morning smell of shower gel and soaps, brewing coffee, and car-exhaust fumes were a recurring routine. Aged between 40 and 80 years old, the respondents felt that their noses had lost their former sensitivity. They apologized: “I’m not very good at describing smells;” “I don’t have a very sensitive nose.” As the world of smells expands and shape-shifts, we have become trapped in a vicious cycle in which olfactory illiteracy and a disinclination to deploy our noses mutually reinforce each other. But when our 130 or so writers were asked about the smells of their past, the responses were revelatory. These miniature essays were magical. As I read them, I was transported into a world that was not my own, yet somehow retained a whiff of the familiar. I would never know these people’s names, but the lovingly crafted descriptions made me feel close to them. To give you just a sniff at this potent prose, it is worth quoting a longer extract: I no longer smell the array of smells I remember from my childhood. A coal fire, the smell of a sweet shop, woodsmoke from a garden, liniment rubbed into youthful limbs before a game of rugby league. Pipe tobacco drifting on the breeze (usually emanating from a man wearing a hat with a little feather in it). Fireworks smelled differently back then, so did our Dads coming home grubby from a day’s graft, welding in a filthy shipyard. The smell from a can of 3 in 1 oil lubricating a bike chain in the shed, a paraffin lamp lighting the same shed. The smell of the candles on the mantelpiece when the lights went out due to the Miners strike in ‘74. I remember the smell of a library book when I got it home and opened its pages for the first time. The smell of my Grandad’s old News of the World when it was a Sunday broadsheet, it smelled so different from my Dad’s Observer, a different ink perhaps. I challenge anybody to remain unmoved by this description. The sense of a past world, with all its minute textures, folds, and creases, is irresistibly palpable. Each time and place has been allocated a scratch-and-sniff label in a personal archive. Smellscapes — the collected smells of the environment in which the writer lived — can tell us a story not just of a single life, but of the world across centuries of change. items.title: The consciousness theory that connects you to everything
items.summary: Neuropsychiatrist Iain McGilchrist turns to one of philosophy’s oldest questions: what is consciousness, and where does it come from? He argues the brain doesn’t create consciousness — it shapes it, the way a larynx shapes air into a voice, filtering a larger field of consciousness into something distinctly yours. From there he builds toward panpsychism, the idea that consciousness pervades everything, from single-cell organisms to mountains. Along the way, he uses the image of a whirlpool in a stream to explain how a stable “self” can exist within constant flow, and makes the case that matter itself is simply a phase of consciousness. items.title: Democrats Are Sounding More Like Republicans
items.summary: For a long time now, Democrats have mostly avoided the language of moral judgment. The average American wasn’t alive when Jimmy Carter inveighed against the “self-indulgence and consumption” of his fellow citizens, and even that seemed to be an aberration. Until this election cycle, that is. Now Senator Chris Murphy is worried about “America’s spiritual unraveling,” and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senate candidate in Michigan, regularly calls out the “moral rot” of the Trump administration. Raphael Warnock and Cory Booker speak in sermon-ese, and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro likes to slap a lectern and say , “I know my Bible!” My favorite example, though, is the Texas Senate candidate James Talarico’s campaign slogan, lifted straight from the gospels with a wink at Jesus’s rebuke to the money changers: “It’s time to start flipping tables.” This is not about finding religion—though faith is a factor : Talarico is one of 12 Democrats who have run for federal office this year who are pastors, former clergy, or seminary students. What is more widespread, rather, is a sudden willingness to speak in universal and absolute terms about norms of behavior—about right and wrong. Post-Carter Democrats have usually presented themselves as the party of technocratic solutions, fetishizing policy or the pragmatic value of—Bill Clinton’s favorite word— triangulation . Now their message sounds like it’s being delivered from a pulpit rather than a bureaucrat’s desk, a moral imperative best summed up in the title of Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear’s new memoir: Go and Do Likewise . I hold one man responsible for this altered tone, and it’s not Jesus. When you have a president whose worldview resembles something out of Squid Game ; who has talked about being constrained only by his “ own morality,” whatever that may be; who characterized soldiers who died for a cause larger than themselves as “suckers” and “losers,” then political physics suggests that the pendulum will soon swing in the other direction. There is a crude and simple way for Democrats to respond to Donald Trump’s flamboyant amorality, and we’re seeing some of it in action. They might simply label everything that he has done (immigration crackdowns, elective wars, tariffs) as “evil,” strongly implying that they are the corrective, the “good.” The Christian right often deploys the language of morality in this Manichaean fashion—it’s the logic by which the evangelist Jerry Falwell once declared Trump to be a “good, moral person.” But the concept quickly cancels itself out when it becomes just another rhetorical weapon. At a rally in Michigan this summer, J. D. Vance said there was something “very, very evil” about El-Sayed —who responded by saying, “Let me tell you what’s evil,” and then cataloged the administration’s policies. To truly name and confront evil—not as just a synonym for things we don’t like but as a foundational concept deeper than day-to-day politics—is, to put it mildly, hard. For people not inclined toward religion, the idea of an ultimate badness seems impossible to extract from theology (an objection I’ll get to). And for those who do have faith, the word might feel too heavy, too spiritually fraught, and too absolute to toss around on the profane battleground of politics. And yet, a working definition of evil might be what we need to recognize what has gone so askew, not just in the current administration but in society, in us. Susan Neiman , the moral philosopher, has titled her new book Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era , but she is quick to explain, on the second page, that “this is not a book about Donald Trump.” What she means is that someone who proudly says that he could shoot someone on 5th Avenue without any repercussions couldn’t triumph in our political system unless the ground was already prepared for him. The evil she wants us to get comfortable naming is more pervasive than just one man or party. And Democrats rushing to counter Trump with righteousness should pay attention. [ Read: Is anything morally obvious anymore? ] Neiman, who has lived mostly in Berlin since the 1980s and served as the director of the Einstein Forum, is a prominent defender of the battered ideals of the Enlightenment. In her books, she has maintained that reason, moral judgment, and the aspiration to universal human dignity—legacies of the early modern thinkers—are worth preserving. They just need some blood flowing through them again. Evil, in particular, has been her special interest for a long time; it was the subject of her most influential book, Evil in Modern Thought , published in 2002. Like Hannah Arendt in her famous book Eichmann in Jerusalem , Neiman is less interested in evil as the province of monsters than as a possibility embedded in ordinary human life. Arendt diagnosed the Nazi bureaucrat Adolf Eichmann with “thoughtlessness,” a habit that can turn mass murder into an administrative task. Neiman builds on this idea in her new book, which is a short, slightly rushed summary of her thinking meant to meet the urgency of the moment. Thoughtlessness is possible, she argues, when morality itself is seen as a joke, as cringe , and when acting out of moral conviction is perceived as a game for suckers and losers. What she names as “the evil that threatens us most today” is “the idea that nothing is evil.” This might sound like a hollow tautology, but to put it another way, she is worried about moral vacuousness. What has shoved aside the notion of good and evil is an ideology of self-interest, which posits that humans are merely animals preoccupied with satisfying their individual needs and increasing their power over others. Or, to borrow the words of that great philosopher Stephen Miller , the idea that “iron laws of the world since the beginning of time” dictate that the planet is governed by “strength,” “force,” and “power” alone. Neiman would identify the kind of thinking Miller expressed as evil: “The signal evil of our age is the belief that self-interest is all that moves us, and ideas of justice are self-deluded hype. Evil actions are those that deny the possibility of morality.” This ideology of self-interest has become so firmly implanted in modern society that someone like Trump could come across simply as the guy who says the quiet part out loud. In her explanation for how we got here, Neiman distributes blame along the entire political spectrum. Her brief against the left is one of negligence. Gradually, beginning in the 1960s, the left abandoned the language of universal principles for a politics focused on identity and power (one of Neiman’s recent books was called Left Is Not Woke ). In place of an objective idea of justice, liberal and leftist thought has resembled something akin to the French philosopher Michel Foucault’s vision of a world of struggle, in which various groups and institutions vie to define reality in terms preferential to themselves. This relativism made morality seem not just irrelevant but also a kind of childish fantasy. And as the left turned away from Enlightenment universalism, the right propagated an equally cold and cutthroat idea, which has shaped how we think about human nature itself. The laissez-faire market fundamentalism promoted by Milton Friedman saw an unregulated market as leading to the best of all possible worlds. For all of the benefits of capitalism, this ethos of competitiveness, taken to its extreme, necessitated a picture of humans as essentially greedy. This idea that people are ruthlessly self-interested and rational, Homo economicus , was supposed to be the basis of a theoretical model, a speculation among early capitalist thinkers such as Adam Smith about how we might act if we were thinking only about maximizing our profit with minimal effort. Yet, Neiman argues, it became accepted not as theory but as truth—that we were “cold-hearted calculators,” as the economist Joseph E. Stiglitz put it. [ Read: What Steph

items.title: Essential Witchy Reads, Recommended by a Witch
items.summary: I am a witch. A kitchen witch, specifically, meaning I make messes into magic and brew potions. Yes, you can drink them . I suppose I’ve always been a witch, but I didn’t embrace that part of myself until about 10 years ago. What happened was I went through some fresh yet familiar trauma, started my life over, found love again, and with it, magic. The inclinations that I’d dismissed, the mythologies I’d thought of in only an academic sense, began to impress themselves upon me. To call me. So, like any good writer or student, I picked up some books on witchcraft. But my initial finds were lackluster, pedestrian. Contextless spells and rootless folklore, presented without acknowledgement of what had been lost in translation. What is modern witchcraft and where did it come from? I wanted to know. First, I uncovered a host of misinformation. For example, the myth of the Burning Times—the idea that actual witches were murdered during the witch trials. (In fact, most victims sentenced to death were hanged, not burned.) The theory was popularized by Margaret Murray, author of The Witch Cult in Western Europe , published in 1921. Murray accepted the testimonies of accused witches as statements of fact, arguing these confessions were valid and not actually extracted under torture, which they definitely were. I learned many modern, widespread witchy practices derive from Wicca, a religion founded by Gerald Gardner, who was heavily influenced by Murray’s work and himself claimed to have uncovered an ancient goddess cult that remained underground during the Christianizing period. A living relic, in other words. Murray wrote the introduction to Gardner’s 1954 book Witchcraft Today . Gardner was also partially inspired by the infamous Aleister Crowley, who didn’t treat women very well, among others. Much of his work would today be considered cultural appropriation. Crowley published The Book of the Law , in which appears the famous phrase, “Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law,” meaning be true to your will and your purpose. The book became the cornerstone of Thelema, a composite religion focused on self-actualization, which Crowley founded in the early 1900s. Thelema still has a small number of followers today. Fun fact: Crowley is the one who replaced the “c” in magic with a “k.” Understanding this history became even more vital once I started the Study Coven , an independent study series for witchy women writers, where I’ve taught classes on witches in literature. My search for texts for the coven brought me to contemporary witches’ memoirs like Initiated by Amanda Yates Garica and hybrid texts like Ariel Gore’s We Were Witches or Pam Grossman’s Waking the Witch , which is both personal and informative. Now my reads were speaking to each other about goddesses, assault, abuse, sex work, and awakening your own power. My students and I culled wisdom from these witches’ stories and insights. For one class, Writing through Ritual, I crafted a syllabus full of writing exercises paired with spells, most of them originals. In the years I’ve been leading the Study Coven, I’ve authored three strange books, including a just-released novel, Witches of the Wheel . It took me around eight years to complete this book. The first drafts were written intuitively, like spellwork, and they were a mess. I was trying to convey something about the experience of magic, and the weight of the divine presence. I wanted to infuse the story itself with power but I had no idea how. It was only through repeated revision, accompanied by intense interrogation of the manuscript, that the book managed to become what it is today. Witches of The Wheel follows Gold, a young woman who can see spirits. After her mother dies and she flees her home, Gold stumbles upon a job at a secret, magical queer bar where there’s never a line for the bathroom and the bottles refill themselves. The bar is also the meeting place for a local coven Gold wants to join. But before she can find her place, she has to contend with an ancient goddess pursuing her, a volatile being with the will to destroy. Here you’ll find a curated list of must-reads for witches. These books have been selected to inspire and educate you, as well as entertain. Together, they do not represent the complete library of witchery. That would be too much for one list. Instead, think of this as the reading for Witches 101. I hope you enjoy this collection. And I hope you’ll find your way to Witches of the Wheel too, particularly if you’re curious about your own powers. Goddess speed! The Conjuring of America by Lindsey Stewart Combining ancestral beliefs with local herbal rituals and remedies, enslaved conjure women employed their magic to midwife babies and effectively address illness. In the process, they passed down vital knowledge and created cures we still rely on today. All this history and more can be found in the pages of The Conjuring of America . This captivating read relies on mythology, meticulous research, and firsthand accounts from enslaved people in order to make a convincing case for the varied influences of conjure in America. Bunny by Mona Awad Samatha Mackey is trapped in a top-tier MFA program, a gentrified oasis in a struggling city. Sam’s peers are a clique of squealing, glittery girl-boss white feminists who like to etch poems on glass and call each other “Bunny.” When the Bunnies’ disdain turns into an invitation to join their girl group, Sam finds the pull of their wealth and splendor too much to resist, even as she risks losing Ava, her one true friend. This novel offers a deftly executed exploration of loneliness and aloneness. Also, you’ve never seen witches like this! And there’s a sequel . Witches, Midwives, and Nurses by Barbara Ehrenreich and Deirdre English Witches, Midwives, and Nurses offers a look at the inherent corruption of the medical establishment and its roots in the persecution of women, particularly as witches. The authors explore how female practitioners were discounted and pushed out of medicine so that men could profit from controlling women’s bodies. First published by the Feminist Press in 1973, Witches, Midwives, and Nurses was groundbreaking in its time, and the latest edition still resonates today in a post-Roe world. The Manningtree Witches by AK Blakemore After their village falls under the spell of a mysterious and aloof witch hunter called Matthew Hopkins (based on a real figure!), young Rebecca and her surly, hard-drinking mother find themselves accused of witchcraft. Ravaged by civil war and hunger, the community is ripe for hysteria and eager for scapegoats to heap blame upon for their misfortunes—and poor, unattached women are the perfect targets. Expertly conjured, The Manningtree Witches is based on historical fact. It’s also written by a fantastic poet and it shows. Initiated by Amanda Yates Garcia This memoir is an underworld odyssey of self-discovery through sex work, poverty, demon love, travel, adventure, and magic. Let the author lead you, and find out how she became the Oracle of LA. This is another one that’s rife with wisdom like: “Witches use magic to compost suffering into something nourishing, something that brings the world around us to life.” Rootwork by Tracy Cross The first book in Cross’s The Conjure Series , Rootwork follows three young sisters sent to their Aunt Teddy’s in Louisiana for the summer. The year is 1889. A matriarch, Aunt Teddy instructs the children in hoodoo and hard life lessons. The girls revel in their newfound freedom, until tragedy strikes. A story of love, revenge, and magic, Rootwork powerfully blends historical fiction, folklore, and horror. Waking the Witch by Pam Grossman An essential overview of modern witchcraft with a bit of memoir mixed in, Waking the Witch examines witchy pop culture archetypes, fairy tales, horror films, and more. items.title: THE RADIANCE Finds Narrative Juice in the Ancient Greeks’ Forms of Love
items.summary: I first encountered Ayad Akhtar’s work when I saw his groundbreaking play Disgraced towards the end of its Broadway run at the Lyceum Theater in New York City and before it won the 2013 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. The night was electric, on-stage and off-stage. I attended the show with my older sister and together we witnessed and heard arguments over the show two blocks away from the theater, presumably from patrons like us, on our way to the subway station. I hadn’t heard that type of heated discussion over a play ever. The polemic on stage literally spilled to the streets. But Akthar is not just a dramatist, he is also an accomplished novelist. His third and latest novel, The Radiance is a departure from his plot-driven Aristotelian dramaturgy. The main character, also named Ayad, gets into a near-fatal car accident in rural New York where he’s set to teach at a university, and this event upends how he views the world. The novel is expansive in form and content, blurring the edges between revelation and madness. It also feels deeply invested in interiority—particularly in how consciousness absorbs and refracts power, ideology, and desire. In our interview, Akhtar and I spoke about the audience, “TikTok dramaturgy” and attention spans, the way he’s dealt with the canon, and how his training in drama influences the way he writes prose. Cherry Lou Sy: I’m a big fan of your playwriting and your prose work. It’s incredible that you’re able to do such high-level work in both, which is rare. How do you decide when something is going to be a play versus a novel? Ayad Akhtar: It’s a great question. With plays, there has to be a sense of immediacy to what you’re doing, it has to translate across the divide between audience and viewer. You don’t have the ability to whisper, if you will, into a reader’s ear the way a novelist can. On stage you can’t really “explain” nuance or overtly convey context. You’ve got to depict it through dialogue and action. Certain kinds just feel more active from jump, requiring less of the viewer or the reader to get involved in—to be more fully immersed. Also, political work, political language, somehow seems to work better in the theater than it does in prose. There’s something about an audience listening to characters talk about something that gives them enough distance to assess it on their own terms, to feel less as if they are being preached to, or persuaded. Rhetoric has an inherent stage value, as we see in Shakespeare endlessly. Both considerations, action and politics, suggest parameters, certain kinds of stories, that make more sense in dramatic form. I’ve been feeling increasingly that readers are less patient, and that they’re less patient with the long crawl of a three-act structure. I would never have known how to do The Radiance as a play. Even though there are play-like elements in it—there are scenes that read like a play—there’s so much context around all of that, I wouldn’t know how to get it to the viewer. CS: I was thinking about how The Radiance is formatted. Can you talk a little about how you decided to plot it, if we can even use that word loosely? AA: A few top-level things. One is that I’ve been feeling increasingly that readers are less patient, and that they’re less patient with the long crawl of a three-act structure. They don’t want to invest in a beginning if they don’t already know what the middle is going to promise, and they’re very eager to figure out what the end is. So there’s a different way of thinking about structure, which is not three-part, beginning, middle, and end, but two-part. It’s about setting a reader’s expectation and then immediately frustrating or fulfilling that expectation and bringing up a new expectation. It’s closer to a kind of TikTok dramaturgy, if you will. I don’t use that tongue in cheek. In Indian classical music there is this idea of the process of getting to the essential juice of the melody—that it takes time to unfold all of the aspects that can eventually allow that juice to be disclosed and savored. One of the things happening with the social media model of narrative construction is that we’re getting to the narrative juice very quickly, with fewer preliminaries, less or almost no build-up. So one of the things I knew I was going to do was tell aspects of this story over and over—not in a strict retelling per se, but advancing the story by reframing and continually disclosing more of it. Each time the story advances, it’s in a sense being re-narrated—now as a legal filing, now as a campus report, now as Lucie’s monologue, now in therapy sessions, etc, etc—and in the process, the arc and implications of the story’s events change, and keep changing. This keeps the story shifting. So the reader always has a live question, not “what happens next” but “what is this story now,” and that tension, I hoped, would carry them through the more demanding passages. The difficulty, I’m hoping, is compensated by absorption. The other structural element I thought a fair bit about is that the book is about love. It’s very clearly about Eros—as there’s much talk about it, but it’s equally about the other “forms” of love as articulated in the Greek philosophical tradition: Agape, or love of one’s fellow person; Storge, or love of kin; and Eros, or desire. The first section tracks a movement through Storge, the second Agape, and the third is Eros. Each ends with a kind of crescendo of that form. So there were lots of structural things I was thinking about in order to tie it together—so that even if the reader didn’t consciously understand what the structure was, there was actually a structure of expectation and fulfillment that they were experiencing, and they wouldn’t get bored. CS: I love that phrase you coined, TikTok dramaturgy. And this telling of the same story in multiple formats made me think of Ovid’s Metamorphoses —this sort of nesting of stories. Then there’s the colonial side. I’m sorry, but I call the storytellers the Ayads: there’s Ayad the writer and Ayad the character. In my head this has been Schrödinger’s Ayad. With Ayad the character, I felt like all of the Western canon was already in one part of his brain, and the colonial or post-colonial brain on the other side. Dare I say the left side? From my reading, it felt like the Western part is the mind and the Eastern part is this spiritual body, and that Ayad the character is trying to reconcile them—and only reconciles through this accident, where he’s forced to jigsaw-puzzle himself back together. AA: That’s a beautiful reading. It reminds me of something I thought about when I was writing the book. Carl Jung has a wonderful memoir called Memories, Dreams, Reflections , where there are so many things he talks about that are remarkable and hard to understand because they seem miraculous. In one of them, he’s visiting a Native American reservation during a trip through the United States, sometime in the ’30s maybe, and he comes across an elder who says something to him that he finds quite remarkable. This is what Jung quotes him as saying, and I’m not going to get this exactly right: “We get confused sometimes when the white man talks about being here (pointing to the head), because we’re here, he said (pointing to the heart). We don’t understand what it is to say that you’re in the head.” I don’t know if I have an ideal reader. I write to the part of myself that is like a kid who doesn’t want to be bored. There are traditions where the intelligence of the heart is the place of unity, where the axial split can be unified.
